If f: X->X is injective then every iterate f^k is injective, so x != x' implies f^k(x) != f^k(x') for all k. Hence an exact recovery (distance returning to 0) of a state perturbation is impossible under injective deterministic dynamics. Non-injectivity is necessary, not sufficient.

Rule 90 on a ring of n cells is linear over GF(2): the difference D evolves as D_t = (x + x^{-1})^t D_0 in GF(2)[x]/(x^n - 1). For n = 2^k, (x + x^{-1})^{n/2} = x^{n/2} + x^{-n/2} = 0 (Frobenius: squaring is additive in characteristic 2, and x^{n/2} = x^{-n/2} mod x^n - 1). For t < n/2, (x+x^{-1})^t has exponents t-2j in (-n/2, n/2), distinct mod n, and the j=0 term has coefficient 1, so it is nonzero. Hence every single-site difference annihilates at exactly t = n/2 (= 8 for n = 16).
Changing f only at vertex s changes the forward orbit of x only if orbit_f(x) contains s. So the set of states whose attractor (or transient) changes is contained in Anc(s) = {x : s in orbit_f(x)}.

The map T: {0,1}^{L} -> {0,1}^{L-1}, T(x)_t = x_t XOR x_{t+1}, satisfies T(x) = T(y) iff y = x or y = complement(x). So every fiber has size 2, H(X | T(X)) = 1 bit under uniform X, and (x_0, T(x)) is a bijection. Entropy rates of a stationary process and of its transition sequence are equal (they differ by at most 1 bit over any block).

In Hamming(7,4) with position-indexed syndrome, a single error at position p has syndrome p (location correctly inferred). A double error at p != q has syndrome p XOR q, which is nonzero and differs from both p and q; the decoder flips a third position, so the inferred location is always wrong and the data may be corrupted (miscorrection). The syndrome identifies a location only under the single-error fault model.

For a first-order Markov process X, I(X_{t+1}; X_{t-1} | X_t) = 0 by the Markov property. Therefore 'history beyond the current state carries predictive information' holds exactly when the process is not first-order Markov in the chosen representation: it is a property of the (process, representation) pair, not of computation in general.

There exists g with P o f = g o P iff for all x, x': P(x) = P(x') implies P(f x) = P(f x') (define g(P x) := P(f x); well-defined exactly under the condition). The coarsest congruence refining ker O is the fixed point of Moore refinement and its block count is the minimum number of states of any deterministic system that reproduces the O-output of every trajectory of f.

For x in {0,1} regarded as integers, Delta x_t = x_{t+1} - x_t equals (1 - 2 x_t) * (x_t XOR x_{t+1}); so the integer first difference is a function of the current state and the GF(2) transition, and carries no additional information. Delta^2 x_t is a function of (x_{t-1}, x_t, x_{t+1}).

For binary alphabets, a 'transition language' (transitions as primary symbols) is the image of the state sequence under the 2-block XOR sliding-block code. It contains no more information than the state sequence (one bit less). What changes is how the information is distributed over time: the finite-context (Markov-order) description of a process can become shorter or longer. Novelty of the concept itself is not supported.

Every attribute of the provisional 'Computational Transition Graph' used so far (states, edges, labels, logical time, perturbation markers) is expressible as a labelled transition system / functional graph plus annotations; no distinct mathematical object has been required.

Masking, information loss and 'minimum surviving information' are all relative to a chosen observable (projection). The same fault is masked for one observable and silent corruption for another; the same dynamics needs 2 or 256 retained states depending on the observable. Cross-layer statements must name the observable.

Normalised perturbation distance is not monotone across the simulated layers (it can grow at the trace layer and shrink at the output layer). This argues against a single linear 'amplification' scale and against assuming a single ordered hierarchy of layers; measurement should be multi-dimensional.
